    41	def layer_weights(T, stage):
    42	    """Pull one DSparkBlock's weights from the loaded tensor dict (GGUF ne order)."""
    43	    p = f"mtp.{stage}."
    44	    w = {
    45	        "hc_attn_fn": T[p + "hc_attn_fn.weight"][0], "hc_attn_scale": T[p + "hc_attn_scale.weight"][0],
    46	        "hc_attn_base": T[p + "hc_attn_base.weight"][0],
    47	        "hc_ffn_fn": T[p + "hc_ffn_fn.weight"][0], "hc_ffn_scale": T[p + "hc_ffn_scale.weight"][0],
    48	        "hc_ffn_base": T[p + "hc_ffn_base.weight"][0],
    49	        "attn_norm": T[p + "attn_norm.weight"][0], "ffn_norm": T[p + "ffn_norm.weight"][0],
    50	        "q_a": T[p + "attn_q_a.weight"][0], "q_a_norm": T[p + "attn_q_a_norm.weight"][0],
    51	        "q_b": T[p + "attn_q_b.weight"][0], "kv": T[p + "attn_kv.weight"][0],
    52	        "kv_a_norm": T[p + "attn_kv_a_norm.weight"][0], "attn_sinks": T[p + "attn_sinks.weight"][0],
    53	        "output_a": T[p + "attn_output_a.weight"][0], "output_b": T[p + "attn_output_b.weight"][0],
    54	        "ffn_gate_inp": T[p + "ffn_gate_inp.weight"][0], "ffn_exp_probs_b": T[p + "exp_probs_b.bias"][0],
    55	        "ffn_gate_shexp": T[p + "ffn_gate_shexp.weight"][0], "ffn_up_shexp": T[p + "ffn_up_shexp.weight"][0],
    56	        "ffn_down_shexp": T[p + "ffn_down_shexp.weight"][0],
    57	    }
    58	    return w

    61	def forward_embed(main_hidden, anchor_tok, main_proj, main_norm, embed_w):
    62	    """mtp.0.forward_embed. main_hidden [3*dim] -> (x [1,block,hc,dim], main_x [1,1,dim])."""
    63	    mh = main_hidden.reshape(1, 1, 3 * DIM).astype(np.float32)
    64	    main_x = rmsnorm(mh @ main_proj.T, main_norm)                  # [1,1,dim] (main_proj HF [out=dim,in=3*dim])
    65	    draft_ids = np.full((1, BLOCK), NOISE_TOK, dtype=np.int64)
    66	    draft_ids[0, 0] = anchor_tok
    67	    # embed_w GGUF ne [dim, vocab]; row token t = embed_w[:, t]. x = embed[draft_ids]
    68	    x = embed_w[draft_ids[0]]                                      # [block, dim] (embed HF [vocab,dim])
    69	    x = x[None]                                                    # [1,block,dim]
    70	    x = np.repeat(x[:, :, None, :], HC, axis=2)                    # [1,block,hc,dim]
    71	    return x.astype(np.float32), main_x
    72	
    73	
    74	def block_forward(x, main_x, input_ids, w, store, stage, start_pos, cos, sin, slot0_kv):
    75	    """DSparkBlock.forward decode (hc_pre -> attn -> hc_post -> hc_pre -> ffn -> hc_post).
    76	    x [1,block,hc,dim], main_x [1,1,dim]. Returns (x', slot1_kv)."""
    77	    # --- attention sub-block ---
    78	    residual = x
    79	    yd, post, comb = hc_pre(x, w["hc_attn_fn"], w["hc_attn_scale"], w["hc_attn_base"])
    80	    yd = rmsnorm(yd, w["attn_norm"])
    81	    w_with_cache = dict(w); w_with_cache["_win_slot0_kv"] = slot0_kv[None] if slot0_kv is not None else None
    82	    attn_out, slot1_kv = dspark_attention(yd, main_x, w_with_cache, start_pos, cos, sin)
    83	    x = hc_post(attn_out, residual, post, comb)
    84	    # --- ffn sub-block ---
    85	    residual = x
    86	    yd, post, comb = hc_pre(x, w["hc_ffn_fn"], w["hc_ffn_scale"], w["hc_ffn_base"])
    87	    yd = rmsnorm(yd, w["ffn_norm"])
    88	    ffn_out = moe(yd, input_ids, w, store)
    89	    x = hc_post(ffn_out, residual, post, comb)
    90	    return x.astype(np.float32), slot1_kv
    91	
    92	
    93	def forward_head(h, anchor_tok, w_head, norm_w, hc_head_fn, hc_head_scale, hc_head_base,
    94	                 markov_w1, markov_w2, conf_proj, lm_head, temp=1.0):
    95	    """mtp.2.forward_head. h [1,block,hc,dim] -> output_ids [block+1], logits [block,vocab]."""
    96	    x = hc_head(h, hc_head_fn, hc_head_scale, hc_head_base)        # [1,block,dim]
    97	    x = rmsnorm(x, norm_w)
    98	    logits = x[0] @ lm_head.T                                       # [block, vocab] (lm_head HF [vocab,dim])
    99	    output_ids = np.zeros(BLOCK + 1, dtype=np.int64)
   100	    output_ids[0] = anchor_tok
   101	    for i in range(BLOCK):
   102	        # markov_head(output_ids[i]): markov_w1 embed [rank], markov_w2 -> [vocab]
   103	        emb = markov_w1[output_ids[i]]                             # [rank]  (markov_w1 HF [vocab,rank])
   104	        bias = emb @ markov_w2.T                                   # [vocab]  (markov_w2 HF [vocab,rank])
   105	        li = (logits[i] + bias) / max(temp, 1e-5)
   106	        output_ids[i + 1] = int(np.argmax(li))
   107	    return output_ids, logits
   108

   110	def forward_spec(T, infos, data_off, main_hidden_prefill, main_hidden_decode, anchor_prefill, anchor_decode,
   111	                 embed_w, lm_head, cos, sin, temp=1.0, prefetch_workers=4):
   112	    """Run a full 2-step drafter scenario: prefill (start_pos=0) caches slot0 KV
   113	    from main_hidden_prefill; decode (start_pos=1) drafts from main_hidden_decode.
   114	    Returns output_ids [block+1]."""
   115	    main_proj = T["mtp.0.main_proj.weight"][0]
   116	    main_norm_w = T["mtp.0.main_norm.weight"][0]
   117	    _, main_x_p = forward_embed(main_hidden_prefill, anchor_prefill, main_proj, main_norm_w, embed_w)
   118	    layers = [layer_weights(T, s) for s in range(3)]
   119	    stores = [ExpertStore(DSPARK_GGUF, infos, data_off, s) for s in range(3)]
   120	    slot0_per_layer = []
   121	    for s in range(3):
   122	        slot0_per_layer.append(dspark_attention_prefill(main_x_p, layers[s], cos, sin))
   123	    x, main_x_d = forward_embed(main_hidden_decode, anchor_decode, main_proj, main_norm_w, embed_w)
   124	    input_ids = np.array([anchor_decode], dtype=np.int64)
   125	    # prefetch the experts each layer will need: route the 5 draft tokens' ffn
   126	    # inputs (post-norm) through the gate; dequant the union of selected experts
   127	    # in parallel. The dense weights needed for the ffn_norm are already in w.
   128	    if prefetch_workers and prefetch_workers > 0:
   129	        from moe import gate
   130	        for s in range(3):
   131	            # compute ffn input: hc_pre -> attn (reuse cached prefill attn is too much;
   132	            # for routing purposes, the pre-norm residual is a good proxy). Use the
   133	            # decode x's mean over hc/block as a representative token.
   134	            probe = x[0].mean(axis=(0, 1))  # [dim]
   135	            _, idx = gate(probe[None, :], layers[s]["ffn_gate_inp"],
   136	                          layers[s]["ffn_exp_probs_b"], 6)
   137	            stores[s].prefetch(idx[0], n_workers=prefetch_workers)
   138	    slot1 = None
   139	    for s in range(3):
   140	        x, slot1 = block_forward(x, main_x_d, input_ids, layers[s], stores[s], s, 1, cos, sin, slot0_per_layer[s])
   141	    out, logits = forward_head(
   142	        x, anchor_decode, None, T["mtp.2.norm.weight"][0],
   143	        T["mtp.2.hc_head_fn.weight"][0], T["mtp.2.hc_head_scale.weight"][0], T["mtp.2.hc_head_base.weight"][0],
   144	        T["mtp.2.markov_head.markov_w1.weight"][0], T["mtp.2.markov_head.markov_w2.weight"][0],
   145	        T["mtp.2.confidence_head.proj.weight"][0], lm_head, temp)
   146	    return out, logits

    11	## Decision rule (pre-registered)
    12	
    13	Primary metric: **held-out p=1 argmax match rate** (the clean, no-rollout signal
    14	from Stage 0), on a dedicated held-out eval set sized for power (≥1 k p=1
    15	positions; the 80-position exactness corpus is too small — +5 pp there is <1 σ).
    16	
    17	- **Reaffirm:** held-out p=1 lifts **≥ +5 pp** AND the overfit-to-eval sanity check
    18	  passes ⇒ a more extensive fine-tune is warranted.
    19	- **Falsify:** full-drafter LoRA (Stage 2b) lifts p=1 **< +1 pp** despite (a) train
    20	  loss converging and (b) the overfit-to-eval check passing ⇒ deficit is
    21	  irreducible by drafter fine-tuning.
    22	- **Inconclusive:** +1–5 pp, or sanity checks fail ⇒ fix impl / broaden data.
    23	
    24	**Tie to Stage 0 ceiling:** head-only training's hard ceiling is the Stage 0
    25	top-2 coverage (~0.91 at p=1). Push toward ~0.88–0.91 ⇒ deficit was output-ordering
    26	(strong reaffirm). Stall ~0.82–0.84 ⇒ head can't discriminate within top-2 ⇒ go
    27	to 2b. Flat ~0.81 ⇒ head cannot help ⇒ go to 2b.
    28	
    29	## Locked setup decisions (this iteration)
    30	
    31	1. **Engine change accepted.** Phase A uses an efficient **`--capture-dataset`
    32	   ds4 mode** (in the ds4 engine repo, this branch) instead of restarting ds4 per
    33	   prompt per layer. Two changes:
    34	   - **Load-once loop** mirroring `--imatrix-dataset` (ds4.c:~25060-25130): one
    35	     model load, iterate prompts, `metal_graph_reset_prefill_state(&g)` between
    36	     prompts, prefill + decode N with `--dump-logprobs` and the dump env set.
    37	   - **Multi-layer comma-list patch** to `metal_graph_debug_wants` (ds4.c:10827,
    38	     currently a single `strtoul` int or `"all"`): accept `"40,41,42"` so one
    39	     generation pass dumps all three tap layers (removes the current 3×
    40	     generation repetition; also shares the per-position Metal sync across layers).
    41	   - Net: **~9× faster capture** (Stage-2 corpus ~110 min → ~13 min; the ~10 s
    42	     model load is paid once, not per invocation).
    43	2. **Few-file sharded storage** (the capture writes *no* per-(layer,pos) `.bin`).
    44	   The `--capture-dataset` mode **buffers per-prompt in engine memory** and writes
    45	   consolidated sharded **safetensors** (see "Storage format" below). Target:
    46	   a handful of shard files + one index, not ~57 k tiny files.
    47	3. **Machine: 128 GB unified memory**, no competing workloads ⇒ the ~23 GB F16
    48	   drafter experts + activations + capture shards all fit with headroom.
    49	4. **Corpus source = three datasets** (downloaded to `issue468/data/corpus_source/`,
    50	   gitignored): `databricks/databricks-dolly-15k` (15 011; general, 8 categories),
    51	   `graycatHCO3/CodeAlpaca-20K-Python` (4 777; Python code), `robdixon/json-extraction`
    52	   (42 884; structured JSON extraction). Spans the exactness corpus's code /
    53	   grounded / synthesis-json genres.
    54	5. **Training env: `issue468/dspark_train/`** — venv (CPython 3.14.3) with
    55	   `torch==2.12.1` (MPS verified), `numpy`, `pyarrow`, `safetensors`, `tqdm`.
    56	   `.venv/`, `checkpoints/`, `runs/`, `data/` gitignored.
    57	
    58	## Architecture — trainable vs frozen
    59	
    60	DSpark drafter (`dspark.gguf`, Q4_K): **518.5 M dense params + 9 packed routed-expert
    61	groups (frozen MoE bulk)**. It borrows the **target's `embed_w` and `lm_head`**
    62	(frozen — not drafter-trainable). Drafter's own output path: `hc_head` (0.07 M) +
    63	`norm` + **`markov_w1`/`markov_w2` (33 M each)** — the markov head dominates the
    64	output side and shapes the top-of-ordering where Stage 0 showed errors concentrate.
    65	
    66	- **Frozen always:** routed MoE experts, target `embed_w`/`lm_head`, attn sinks.
    67	- **Stage 2a (head-only):** LoRA on `hc_head` + `markov_w1`/`markov_w2` + learnable
    68	  `norm` scale; everything upstream **precomputed** (frozen drafter forward) ⇒ no
    69	  MoE/attn in the training loop (tiny, fast, near-zero port risk).
    70	- **Stage 2b (full-drafter):** add LoRA on `main_proj` (50 M) + 3 layers' dense
    71	  attn (`q_a`/`q_b`/`kv`/`output_a`/`output_b`) and shared-expert FFN
    72	  (`gate_shexp`/`up_shexp`/`down_shexp`) + the head. Routed experts still frozen.
    73	
    74	## Storage format (few-file, sharded)
    75	
    76	Consolidated **safetensors** shards (memmap-able, torch-native). Per shard:
    77	- `main_hidden` `[N, 12288]` **float16** — drafter input (layers 40/41/42 concat), per anchor position.
    78	- `token_ids` `[N]` int32 — target greedy argmax stream (K-step targets derived by windowing at train time).
    79	- `topk_ids` `[N, 128]` int32 + `topk_logits` `[N, 128]` float16 — for optional soft-label KL and the Stage-0-style rank diagnostic on the fine-tuned drafter.
    80	- `prompt_idx` `[N]` int32, `pos_in_prompt` `[N]` int32 — boundaries.
    81	Plus one small `index.json` (prompt_idx → source dataset, prompt-text ref, prompt_tokens).
    82	Layout: **train → ~4 shards, eval → 1 shard** (~5 files + index). Sizing at 180
    83	train × 128 pos: ~0.57 GB `main_hidden` + ~18 MB topk; eval ~one-fifth. Stored in
    84	`issue468/dspark_train/data/` (gitignored; referenced in STATUS/inventory).
    85

   118	## Apple Silicon / PyTorch specifics
   119	
   120	- `torch.device("mps")`; F16/BF16 matmul supported on M-series (verified: 2.12.1).
   121	  F32 master for LoRA params. CPU fallback for any op MPS dislikes.
   122	- Experts: dequant once to F16, frozen, **kept out of the autograd graph**.
   123	- Teacher-forcing vs inference exposure bias: only p=1 is bias-free (prev=anchor).
   124	  Train on all K (teacher-forced) but **decide on p=1**; report deeper positions
   125	  as secondary.
   126	- Drafter borrows target `lm_head`/`embed_w` — do **not** train them.

   141	## Open questions (need resolution before/during execution)
   142	
   143	1. **Soft vs hard labels.** Hard-label CE directly optimizes the argmax metric;
   144	   top-128 KL generalizes better. *Recommendation:* hard-CE + label smoothing
   145	   (0.1) primary, soft-KL as an ablation. *(user confirm)*
   146	2. **Is frozen-experts conclusive enough?** A null with experts frozen leaves
   147	   "expert tuning" as an untested escape hatch — i.e. it falsifies "dense/head
   148	   LoRA fine-tune," not "any fine-tune." Do we accept that boundary, or add a
   149	   **Stage 2c** (partial expert tuning) for a harder falsification? *(user decision
   150	   — affects how conclusive "stop" can be)*
   151	3. **LoRA rank / param boundary.** Default rank 32 on the dense projections +
   152	   markov head. Tunable; raise if 2a/2b underfit. *(default 32)*
   153	4. **Include the crossed-oracle diagnostic before training?** *Recommendation: yes*
   154	   — it's cheap and tells us input-vs-label localization upfront. *(user confirm)*
   155	5. **Generation length per prompt.** 128 (default) vs 256 (more data, cheap now
   156	   that capture is fast). *(default 128)*
   157	6. **Loss weighting across K positions.** Equal (standard MTP) vs p=1-weighted.
   158	   *(default equal; monitor per-position)*
   159	7. **temp>0 capture.** PoC decides on temp=0 (greedy, exactness). Note the speedup
   160	   model's caveat that temp 0.5/1.0 lowers E[a]. *(default temp=0; temp>0 = future)*
   161	8. **Throughput-gate coupling (scope boundary).** This PoC measures **acceptance**
   162	   only. The GOAL's +20 % throughput gate *also* needs the unbuilt anchor-reuse
   163	   verifier (`spec_speedup_model.md`). So reaffirm = "acceptance improves"
   164	   (necessary, not sufficient for the throughput gate). *(note, not blocking)*
   165	
   166	## What each outcome means for the program
   167	
   168	- **Reaffirm:** open a full Stage 2 — larger corpus, higher rank / partial-expert
   169	  tuning, integrate with the anchor-reuse verifier; realistic target the secondary
   170	  gate, outside shot at +20 %.
   171	- **Falsify:** close the fine-tuning direction; redirect to server-side batching
   172	  (amortize the verify bandwidth floor) or accept local single-request speculative

     1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
     2	"""Measure oracle draft-prefix agreement against one retained target bundle.
     3	
     4	For temp=0 this is greedy-prefix agreement against the deterministic target
     5	stream. For temp>0 it is sampled-stream prefix agreement against the retained
     6	selected target continuation from the same seeded run.
     7	
     8	This module exposes three pieces so a bulk runner can amortize the expensive
     9	one-time loads (target embed/lm_head, drafter dense tensors, RoPE) across many
    10	bundles and many drafter GGUFs without re-spawning a process per bundle:
    11	
    12	  - build_model_ctx(model_path)   : load target embed_w + lm_head + RoPE once
    13	  - build_drafter_ctx(dspark_path): load drafter dense tensors + layers + stores
    14	  - measure_bundle(bundle_dir, mctx, dctx) : run one bundle, return summary dict
    15	
    16	The CLI main() builds both contexts from args and calls measure_bundle, so the
    17	single-bundle path is behaviour-identical to the bulk path (single source of
    18	truth for the measurement numerics).

    57	def load_mh(bundle_dir: Path, pos: int) -> np.ndarray | None:
    58	    packed = bundle_dir / "oracle" / CANONICAL_INPUTS
    59	    if packed.exists():
    60	        data = np.load(packed)
    61	        positions = data["positions"]
    62	        hits = np.where(positions == pos)[0]
    63	        if hits.size:
    64	            return data["main_hidden"][int(hits[0])]
    65	    path = bundle_dir / "oracle" / f"main_hidden_pos{pos}.npy"
    66	    if not path.exists():
    67	        return None
    68	    return np.load(path)

    70	
    71	def dspark_attn(x_draft: np.ndarray, win_kv: np.ndarray, n_real: int,
    72	                w: dict, cos: np.ndarray, sin: np.ndarray, start_pos: int) -> np.ndarray:
    73	    bs = 1
    74	    block = x_draft.shape[1]
    75	    scale = HEAD_DIM ** -0.5
    76	    qr = rmsnorm(x_draft @ w["q_a"].T, w["q_a_norm"])
    77	    q = (qr @ w["q_b"].T).reshape(bs, block, N_HEADS, HEAD_DIM)
    78	    q = q * (1.0 / np.sqrt(np.mean(q * q, axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-6))
    79	    cs = cos[start_pos + 1:start_pos + 1 + block]
    80	    ss = sin[start_pos + 1:start_pos + 1 + block]
    81	    q[..., -ROPE_DIM:] = apply_rotary(q[..., -ROPE_DIM:], cs[None, :, None, :], ss[None, :, None, :])
    82	    kv = rmsnorm(x_draft @ w["kv"].T, w["kv_a_norm"])
    83	    kv[..., -ROPE_DIM:] = apply_rotary(kv[..., -ROPE_DIM:], cs[None, :, :], ss[None, :, :])
    84	    kv_all = np.concatenate([win_kv[None], kv], axis=1)
    85	    idx = np.concatenate([np.arange(n_real), WIN + np.arange(block)])
    86	    kv_g = np.broadcast_to(kv_all[:, idx], (1, block, idx.size, HEAD_DIM))
    87	    o = sparse_attn(q, kv_g, w["attn_sinks"], scale)
    88	    o[..., -ROPE_DIM:] = apply_rotary(o[..., -ROPE_DIM:], cs[None, :, None, :], -ss[None, :, None, :])
    89	    gd = HEAD_DIM * N_HEADS // N_GROUPS
    90	    o_g = o.reshape(bs, block, N_GROUPS, gd)
    91	    wo_a = w["output_a"].reshape(N_GROUPS, O_LORA, gd)
    92	    o_lor = np.einsum("bsgd,grd->bsgr", o_g, wo_a)
    93	    return (o_lor.reshape(bs, block, N_GROUPS * O_LORA) @ w["output_b"].T).astype(np.float32)

    96	def build_model_ctx(model_path: str) -> dict:
    97	    """Load target-model-derived tensors that are independent of the drafter GGUF.
    98	    Load once, reuse across every drafter and every bundle."""
    99	    _, ti, tdo = index_gguf(model_path)
   100	    embed_w = read_tensor(model_path, ti, tdo, "token_embd.weight").astype(np.float32)
   101	    lm_head = read_tensor(model_path, ti, tdo, "output.weight").astype(np.float32)
   102	    cos, sin = precompute_rope(64, 4096)
   103	    return {"embed_w": embed_w, "lm_head": lm_head, "cos": cos, "sin": sin}
   104

   106	def build_drafter_ctx(dspark_path: str) -> dict:
   107	    """Load drafter-specific dense tensors + per-layer weight dicts + expert stores.
   108	    Load once per drafter GGUF, reuse across every bundle."""
   109	    _, T, infos, doff, _ = load_gguf_dense_only(dspark_path)
   110	    return {
   111	        "T": T,
   112	        "infos": infos,
   113	        "doff": doff,
   114	        "main_proj": T["mtp.0.main_proj.weight"][0],
   115	        "main_norm_w": T["mtp.0.main_norm.weight"][0],
   116	        "layers": [layer_weights(T, s) for s in range(3)],
   117	        "stores": [ExpertStore(dspark_path, infos, doff, s) for s in range(3)],
   118	    }

   121	def measure_bundle(bundle_dir: Path, mctx: dict, dctx: dict, *, candidate: str | None = None) -> dict:
   122	    """Run the drafter forward over one retained bundle and return the acceptance

   148	        mkv[..., -ROPE_DIM:] = apply_rotary(mkv[..., -ROPE_DIM:], cos[0], sin[0])
   149	        win_kv[s][0] = mkv[0, 0]

   157

   159	        pos = pos0 + step
   160	        anchor = int(target_tokens[step])
   161	        mh = load_mh(bundle_dir, pos)
   162	        if mh is None:
   163	            break
   164	        main_x = rmsnorm(mh.reshape(1, 1, 3 * DIM) @ main_proj.T, main_norm_w)
   165	        for s in range(3):

   167	            mkv[..., -ROPE_DIM:] = apply_rotary(mkv[..., -ROPE_DIM:], cos[step], sin[step])

   177	            yd = rmsnorm(yd, layers[s]["attn_norm"])
   178	            ao = dspark_attn(yd, win_kv[s], n_real, layers[s], cos, sin, step)
   179	            x = hc_post(ao, res, post, comb)
   180	            res = x
   181	            yd, post, comb = hc_pre(x, layers[s]["hc_ffn_fn"], layers[s]["hc_ffn_scale"], layers[s]["hc_ffn_base"])
   182	            yd = rmsnorm(yd, layers[s]["ffn_norm"])

   195	            T["mtp.2.confidence_head.proj.weight"][0],
   196	            lm_head,

   199	        draft = [int(v) for v in out[1:].tolist()]
   200	        target = [int(v) for v in target_tokens[step + 1:step + 1 + BLOCK]]
   201	        match = sum(1 for d, t in zip(draft, target) if d == t)
   202	        prefix = 0
   203	        for i, (d, t) in enumerate(zip(draft, target)):
   204	            if d == t:
   205	                prefix = i + 1
   206	            else:
   207	                break
   208	        prefix_hist[prefix] += 1
   209	        total_match += match
   210	        total_pos += BLOCK
   211	        rows.append({
   212	            "step": step,
   213	            "position": pos,
   214	            "anchor": anchor,
   215	            "draft": draft,
   216	            "target": target,
   217	            "match": match,
   218	            "prefix": prefix,
   219	        })
   220	
   221	    n_rows = len(rows)
   222	    avg_prefix = float(sum(row["prefix"] for row in rows) / n_rows) if n_rows else 0.0
   223	    summary = {
   224	        "label": label,
   225	        "candidate": candidate,
   226	        "bundle_dir": str(bundle_dir),
   227	        "prompt_name": manifest["prompt_name"],
   228	        "temperature": manifest["temperature"],
   229	        "seed": manifest["seed"],
   230	        "prompt_tokens": manifest["prompt_tokens"],
   231	        "measure_steps": n_rows,
   232	        "total_positions": total_pos,
   233	        "total_match": total_match,
   234	        "match_pct": (100.0 * total_match / total_pos) if total_pos else 0.0,
   235	        "average_prefix": avg_prefix,
   236	        "prefix_hist": prefix_hist,
   237	        "rows": rows,
   238	        "reference_mode": "greedy" if float(manifest["temperature"]) == 0.0 else "sampled-stream",
   239	    }
   240	    return summary
   241	
   242	
   243	def main() -> int:
   244	    args = parse_args()
   245	    mctx = build_model_ctx(args.model)
   246	    dctx = build_drafter_ctx(args.dspark)
   247	    summary = measure_bundle(Path(args.bundle_dir), mctx, dctx)
   248	    if args.json_out:
   249	        Path(args.json_out).write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=2) + "\n")
   250	    else:
   251	        print(json.dumps(summary, indent=2))
   252	    return 0
   253	
   254	
   255	if __name__ == "__main__":
   256	    raise SystemExit(main())

     1	# Speculative-decode speedup model — DSPark drafter on the ds4 target
     2	
     3	Date: 2026-07-06 (cycle-cost corrected per reviewer). Numpy projection of
     4	speculative-decode speedup answering three questions. Model:
     5	`issue468/model_spec_speedup.py`; outputs:
     6	`issue48/artifacts/spec_speedup_model/{summary.json,model_inputs.json}`.
     7	
     8	## Model (corrected cycle accounting)
     9	
    10	The verifier forward produces the correction/bonus token at the rejection point,
    11	and that token **is the anchor for the next cycle**. A fresh anchor decode is
    12	needed **only on full-block acceptance** (no rejection point). Therefore:
    13	
    14	```
    15	cost(reject)      = draft + verify                 (verify yields the anchor)
    16	cost(full accept) = draft + verify + decode
    17	E[cost/cycle]     = draft + verify_ms(K) + decode * P(full accept)
    18	                  = draft + verify_ms(K) + decode * S(K)     # S(K)=P(first K all match)
    19	E[tokens/cycle]   = E[a|K] + 1                      # +1 = correction bonus or fresh decode
    20	speedup(K)        = (E[a|K] + 1) * decode_ms / E[cost]
    21	```
    22	
    23	Inputs (all retained/measured): `decode_ms=26` (1000/38.49 t/s), `draft_ms=10`
    24	(DSpark, given), `verify_ms(K)` = cross-prompt median of `mtp_verifier_bench_long`
    25	(K2:43.6, K3:59.7, K4:65.8, K5:74.5, K6:79.6), acceptance = greedy prefix
    26	histogram (temp=0) from `exactness_small_bundles`: S(1..5)=0.8125, 0.65, 0.425,
    27	0.2875, 0.1625; E[a|K]=1.4625/1.8875/2.175/2.3375 for K=2/3/4/5.
    28	
    29	**Important distinction:** this is an *optimized-verifier* projection. The
    30	shipped `ds4 --mtp` implementation pays a separate anchor decode **every** cycle
    31	(decode+draft+verify), which is why measured MTP t/s is much worse (see
    32	`mtp_verifier_bench_results.md`). Building the verifier to reuse the
    33	verify-produced anchor is itself worth ~18 pp at K=4 (moves K=4 from ~−19% to
    34	~−1%). That verifier-implementation change is a real lever, independent of the
    35	drafter.
    36	
    37	## Adversarial review (codex / gpt-5.5, xhigh) — strong perspective, retained
    38	
    39	The findings below (Q1/Q2/Q3) are computed **under the explicit modeling
    40	assumption that the verifier reuses the anchor** (per the brief). A read-only
    41	adversarial review was run with `codex exec -m gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort=xhigh`;
    42	retained at `issue468/artifacts/spec_speedup_model/codex_review.md` (prompt
    43	`codex_review_prompt.md`, full trace `codex_review_output.txt`). Codex was **not**
    44	given the anchor-reuse context, so its central attack lands on that assumption
    45	itself. Its perspective is recorded here as the primary caveat; it does not
    46	retract the under-assumption findings.
    47	
    48	**On the assumption (codex's load-bearing objection).** Codex argues anchor-reuse
    49	is the unverified risk: on rejection the verify forward yields the correction
    50	token's *logits* but has not run the target on that token, so there is no valid
    51	KV/hidden state to anchor the next draft (the verify processed the *rejected*
    52	draft at that position). It verified this against the code: every shipped
    53	speculative cycle starts with `ds4_session_eval(first_token)` (`ds4.c:27202`) and
    54	committed state covers only processed drafts (`ds4.c:27555`), i.e. the current
    55	`--mtp` path decodes every cycle. **Under the shipped verifier the cost reverts to
    56	`decode+draft+verify`, giving K=4 = −18.9% and a ~88% per-position requirement to
    57	beat baseline** (vs −0.9% / ~79% under the reuse assumption). Realizability note:
    58	reusing the anchor is *possible in principle* — folding the correction into the
    59	next verify forward replaces the 26 ms decode with ~verify_ms(K+1)−verify_ms(K)
    60	≈ 9 ms — but it is unbuilt on ds4 and not free of overhead. The codex-proposed
    61	**falsifier**: force a rejection and try to start the next draft without decoding
    62	the correction; divergence ⇒ reuse is not realizable on this graph.
    63	
    64	**Sensitivities that hold even under the reuse assumption (in-scope):**
    65	- **Residual per-cycle overhead set to zero.** Measured MTP cycle at K=4 is
    66	  `total − draft − verify ≈ 42 ms`; removing the ~26 ms anchor decode still leaves
    67	  ~15–19 ms of readback / partial-accept rollback / first-miss waste. A
    68	  reuse-optimized verifier still pays some of this; adding ~10 ms drops the
    69	  under-assumption K=4 speedup from 0.991 to ~0.885. So the break-even is fragile
    70	  to overhead even granting anchor reuse.
    71	- **The "~2 pp" precision is statistically indefensible.** Across the 10 prompts
    72	  E[a|4] has sd ≈ 0.43 (prompt-level 95% half-width ±0.3) vs a 0.028 drafts/cycle
    73	  break-even gap; per-prompt modeled K=4 spans −18.5% to +10.6%. The mean figure
    74	  is inside the noise.
    75	- **Acceptance-data caveats:** measured on 67–165-token prompts along the
    76	  drafter's own greedy spine, not real trajectories (post-rejection cycles start
    77	  from an unpredicted correction token — likely lower acceptance); temp 0.5/1.0
    78	  drops E[a|4] from 2.175 to ~1.92 (~7 pp hit).
    79	- **Q3 "cannot help" is too absolute:** a depth-3 4-node tree could clear +20%
    80	  *if* its verify fell to ≤~51 ms and acceptance were near-perfect — neither met
    81	  today, but the ceiling isn't literally zero.
    82	- **draft=10 ms** leaves only ~0.7 ms of cost headroom at K=4 under the reuse
    83	  model (+1 ms draft → ~−2%, +5 ms → ~−6.5%).
    84	
    85	**Net:** the Q1/Q2/Q3 results below are valid *conditional on anchor reuse and
    86	low residual overhead*. Codex's review flags those two conditions as the
    87	load-bearing, unverified risks (plus the acceptance/noise caveats). Treat the
    88	under-assumption numbers as the optimistic edge of a band whose pessimistic edge
    89	(~−19% at K=4) is the shipped-verifier reality.
    90	
    91	## Q2 — does K=4 give a speedup? ~Break-even (−0.9%), not yet a gain.
    92	
    93	| K | verify_ms | P(full) | cycle_ms | E[a\|K] | speedup | vs base |
    94	|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
    95	| 1 | 26.0 | 0.812 | 57.1 | 0.812 | 0.825 | −17.5% |
    96	| 2 | 43.6 | 0.650 | 70.5 | 1.462 | 0.908 | −9.2% |
    97	| 3 | 59.7 | 0.425 | 80.8 | 1.888 | 0.930 | −7.0% |
    98	| 4 | 65.8 | 0.288 | 83.3 | 2.175 | **0.991** | **−0.9%** |
    99	| 5 | 74.5 | 0.163 | 88.7 | 2.338 | 0.978 | −2.2% |
   100	
   101	At current acceptance every K is still net-negative, but **K=4 is essentially at
   102	break-even (−0.9%)** and K=5 close (−2.2%). The optimum is K=4. So with a
   103	correctly-built verifier the current drafter is right at the threshold — a small
   104	acceptance gain flips it positive.
   105	
   106	## Q1 — acceptance needed to beat baseline and to clear +20%
   107	
   108	`E beat`/`E +20%` = accepted drafts/cycle needed (uses actual S(K) for the
   109	full-accept decode); `p` = uniform per-position match probability (geometric)
   110	achieving it; `-1` = unreachable (ceiling below target).
   111	
   112	| K | E beat | E +20% | p beat | p +20% | current E | current p |
   113	|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
   114	| 2 | 1.712 | 2.254 | **unreachable** | **unreachable** | 1.462 | 0.809 |
   115	| 3 | 2.106 | 2.727 | 0.890 | **unreachable** | 1.888 | 0.786 |
   116	| 4 | 2.203 | 2.843 | **0.792** | 0.940 | 2.175 | 0.771 |
   117	| 5 | 2.412 | 3.095 | 0.783 | 0.890 | 2.338 | 0.757 |
   118	
   119	- **Beat baseline:** K=4 needs p≈0.79 (current 0.771 → **+2 pp**), i.e. E[a|4]
   120	  2.20 vs current 2.175 (+0.03 drafts/cycle). K=5 needs p≈0.78 (+2.6 pp). K=2
   121	  cannot beat baseline at any acceptance (its perfect-accept ceiling is −2%);
   122	  K=3 can (ceiling +8.7%) but not the +20% gate.
   123	- **+20% gate:** K=4 needs p≈0.94 (+17 pp); **K=5 needs the least lift, p≈0.89
   124	  (+13 pp)**, because its higher ceiling (+41% vs +28%) amortizes the verify
   125	  better. The gate is reachable in principle (K≥4 ceilings exceed +20%) but
   126	  needs a substantially better drafter.
   127	
   128	So: **the current drafter is ~2 pp of per-position acceptance away from beating
   129	baseline at K=4**, and ~13-17 pp away from the +20% gate. The gap is acceptance,
   130	not structure.
   131	
   132	## Q3 — can a 4-node draft tree give a speedup? NO.
   133	
   134	A verify of N nodes costs `verify_ms(N)` regardless of tree shape (bandwidth
   135	floor). A branched tree has max committed depth d < N; a linear chain has d = N.
   136	Ceilings = max speedup at **perfect** acceptance:
   137	
   138	| N nodes | verify_ms | linear d=N ceiling | best tree d=N−1 ceiling |
   139	|---:|---:|---:|---:|
   140	| 3 | 59.7 | +8.7% | −18.5% |
   141	| **4** | 65.8 | **+27.7%** | **+2.2%** |
   142	| 5 | 74.5 | +41.2% | +17.6% |
   143	| 6 | 79.6 | +57.4% | +34.9% |
   144	
   145	For a **4-node** structure (corrected cost):
   146	- **linear depth-4**: ceiling +27.7%; at current acceptance E=2.175 → **0.991
   147	  (−0.9%)**.
   148	- **tree depth-3 (spine3 + repair at pos 3)**: ceiling **+2.2%** even at perfect
   149	  acceptance. At current top-1 (no repair lift) → 0.864 (−13.6%); **with a
   150	  perfect repair branch** → 0.873 (−12.7%) — i.e. even a flawless repair leaves
   151	  it ~12% below baseline and worse than linear-4.
   152	- **tree depth-2 (spine2 + 2 leaves)**: ceiling −23.4% (always slower).
   153	
   154	Two independent reasons trees lose here:
   155	1. **Ceiling:** a 4-node tree's perfect-acceptance ceiling is +2.2% (below the
   156	   +20% gate and barely above baseline), because branches spend verify nodes
   157	   without extending the committed prefix.
   158	2. **Hedging is dominated by spine extension** — and is *doubly* penalized: the
   159	   4th node as a spine extension adds E = S(4) = 0.288; as a position-3 hedge it
   160	   adds only E = S(2)·Δ ≈ 0.065/0.130/0.195 for a +10/20/30% top-2 lift (spine
   161	   wins at every realistic lift). Worse, raising pos-3 coverage *also* raises
   162	   P(full-block-acceptance), so it increases the fresh-anchor-decode penalty —
   163	   which is why the perfect-repair tree (0.873) barely beats the no-repair tree
   164	   (0.864).
   165	
   166	**Best tree strategy:** do not branch — use a linear chain. If branching is
   167	forced, maximize depth (spine N−1 + one repair at the deepest node), but no
   168	4-node tree beats the gate or delivers a real speedup.
   169	
   170	## Conclusions
   171	
   172	1. **Q1:** with an optimized verifier, beating baseline needs only ~79%
   173	   per-position acceptance at K=4 (current ~77% → **~2 pp short**); the +20%
   174	   gate needs ~89-94% (K=5/K=4) → ~13-17 pp short.
   175	2. **Q2:** K=4 is at **break-even (−0.9%)** with the current drafter and an
   176	   optimized verifier — not a gain yet, but a ~2 pp acceptance improvement makes
   177	   it beat baseline. (The shipped `--mtp` implementation is far worse because it
   178	   pays a redundant anchor decode every cycle.)
   179	3. **Q3:** a 4-node draft tree cannot give a speedup — ceiling +2.2%, current
   180	   ~−13%, dominated by a linear chain. Hedging is doubly penalized (wastes verify
   181	   nodes AND raises the full-accept decode penalty).
   182	
   183	Net: the binding constraint is **drafter acceptance** (precision is exhausted per
   184	`dspark_quantization_ceiling.md`). Two realistic levers: (a) a verifier that
   185	reuses the verify-produced anchor (the ds4 `--mtp` implementation does not — this
   186	is ~18 pp at K=4), and (b) a materially better drafter. Trees do not help.
   187	
   188	## Caveats
   189	
   190	- `verify_ms(K)` is the MTP verifier cost; DSPark would reuse the same target
   191	  verifier. Tree-attention verify may be marginally cheaper (sparser masks) but
   192	  the bandwidth floor is unchanged, so the +2.2% tree ceiling is robust.
   193	- Acceptance is the retained greedy (temp=0) prefix distribution over 5-token
   194	  blocks; K>5 is not grounded. The corrected cost uses S(K)=P(first K all match).
   195	- The geometric per-position `p` is a summary statistic; real acceptance decays
   196	  faster with depth (non-geometric), making the gate modestly harder than the
   197	  uniform-p numbers suggest.
   198	- The optimized-verifier projection assumes the verify forward produces a usable
   199	  anchor hidden state at the rejection point; this is standard but is an
   200	  implementation property to confirm against the ds4 graph (the current `--mtp`
   201	  path does not do it).

    11	## Question (gated by Stage 0)
    12	
    13	Stage 0 showed drafter p=1 misses are **shallow** (median target-rank 1.0; 100%
    14	within top-10). Stage 1 tests the specific mechanism: does **raising tap-layer
    15	precision convert those rank-2 misses into rank-1 matches** — i.e. is the mismatch
    16	localized to the drafter's tap layers (40/41/42) and quant-driven? (Codex flagged
    17	this as a partial proxy for the decisive FP-teacher test, which needs a model we
    18	don't have locally.)
    19	
    20	## Setup — clean A/B
    21	
    22	- **Baseline:** retained IQ2XXS bundles (`exactness_small_bundles/*__t0p0`).
    23	- **Variant:** `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Layers37-42Q4KExperts-...-imatrix-fixed.gguf` —
    24	  same model, **layers 37–42 routed experts at Q4_K** (everything else IQ2XXS),
    25	  same AProjQ8/SExpQ8/OutQ8 (so embed/lm_head quant unchanged).
    26	- Same 10 prompts, temp=0, seed=2, ctx=4096, 14 generated tokens. Greedy is
    27	  seed-independent, so tokenization matches (prompt_tokens identical per prompt).
    28	- Re-captured layer 40/41/42 hidden states + greedy tokens + top-128 from the
    29	  Q4-tap target, then re-measured drafter acceptance on the fresh captures. **The
    30	  drafter, its weights, and embed/lm_head quant are unchanged** — only the target
    31	  (hidden states the drafter sees + the ground-truth tokens) changes.
    32	
    33	**Freshness verified (contract):** Q4-tap `main_hidden` differs from baseline
    34	(max abs diff 59.5, mean 1.09, not identical); 33/140 target tokens differ — the
    35	captures are genuinely from the Q4-tap run, not reused.
    36	
    37	## Result
    38	
    39	| metric | IQ2XXS baseline | Q4-tap | Δ |
    40	|---|---:|---:|---:|
    41	| **E[a\|5block]** (avg accepted prefix) | 2.3375 | 2.4375 | **+0.10** |
    42	| **p=1 match rate** (clean signal, n=80) | 0.8125 | 0.7875 | **−0.025** |
    43	| overall match% (all 5 positions) | 51.0% | 54.0% | +3.0 pp |
    44	| per-prompt avg-prefix direction | — | — | 4 up / 3 down / 3 flat |
    45	
    46	**The clean signal (p=1) is flat-to-slightly-negative** (65/80 → 63/80 matches;
    47	McNemar discordants 7 base-only / 5 q4-only, p≈0.77; not significant). The +0.10
    48	E[a|5block] is **statistically indistinguishable from zero** (paired t p=0.54;
    49	per-prompt bootstrap 95% CI **[−0.16, +0.41]** — wide, straddling zero) — so it is
    50	NOT proven noise; the study is underpowered to detect a small effect. There is a
    51	**one-sided per-position trend**: Q4-tap is flat/slightly-negative at p=1
    52	(−2.5 pp), unchanged at p=2, and increasingly positive deeper (p=3 +3.75, p=4
    53	+5.0, p=5 +8.75 pp) — but deeper positions are rollout-confounded (after the first
    54	miss the drafter's context diverges) and small-N, so this is an observation, not a
    55	clean effect. **Net: this Q4-tap expert-only variant does not materially improve
    56	the clean p=1 acceptance; any broader claim is limited by power and by the
    57	variant's partial precision (see caveats).**
    58	
    59	## Interpretation (softened per adversarial review)
    60	
    61	- **This Q4-tap variant does not materially help p=1; broader falsification is
    62	  overstated.** The drafter's input layers (40/41/42) were raised to Q4-K experts,
    63	  yet p=1 acceptance did not improve. But this only falsifies *"this expert-only
    64	  Q4-tap variant materially helps"* — **not** *"tap-localized quant mismatch"* in
    65	  general: layers 40–42 still receive Q2-corrupted activations from below
    66	  (layers 1–39 unchanged), so a flat result is ambiguous between (a) lower-layer
    67	  Q2 effects, (b) drafter-vs-target calibration error independent of quant, and
    68	  (c) a real but small effect the study was underpowered to detect.
    69	- **Serving a higher-precision target is not demonstrated as a usable lever** at
    70	  this precision level and sample size. (Resolving localization cleanly needs a
    71	  full Q8/BF16 target — codex's proposed decisive test — not available locally.)
    72	- **Fine-tuning is a plausible next lever, not a proven exclusive one.** The
    73	  Stage 0 top-2 coverage (≈0.91 at p=1) is **headroom** (target currently sits at
    74	  drafter rank ≤2 ~91% of the time), NOT a hard fine-tune ceiling — a fine-tune
    75	  could do better or worse. It indicates the drafter is consistently in the right
    76	  neighborhood, which is the regime where a fine-tune has leverage, but only an
    77	  actual fine-tune (Stage 2) would measure the realized gain. Reframing the
    78	  deficit as "calibration error" is an inference beyond the data (the data shows
    79	  shallow disagreement, not its cause).
    80	
    81	## Caveats
    82	
    83	- The Q4-tap variant raises only layers 37–42 experts; lower layers stay IQ2XXS,
    84	  so a genuinely flat result cannot distinguish "not quant" from "quant but in
    85	  lower layers." Resolving that needs a full Q8/BF16 target (not available locally).
    86	- n=10 prompts, 8 measure steps each (80 p=1 positions). The +0.10 E[a|5block] and
    87	  −0.025 p=1 are both within noise; the robust claim is "no material effect," not
    88	  a precise negative magnitude.
    89	- Both runs are temp=0 (greedy). temp>0 deployment trajectories were not tested.
    90	
    91	## What this means for the Stage 2 decision
    92	
    93	Stage 0 + Stage 1 together: the acceptance deficit is **shallow and in the right
    94	neighborhood (Stage 0, robust)**, and **not cleanly attributable to tap-layer
    95	precision (Stage 1, underpowered + partial-precision variant)**. A drafter
    96	fine-tune on the served target's distribution remains a **plausible** lever with
    97	meaningful headroom (top-2 coverage ≈0.91 at p=1), but it is **not proven** as the
    98	exclusive or sufficient path, and the realized gain is unknown until Stage 2.
    99	See the final recommendation.
   100

The capture path does not make the comma-list patch “trivial”: the current dump helper gates one layer via `strtoul`, and every actual dump synchronizes and starts a new command batch. I’m now quantifying the paired-test power under explicit discordance assumptions because McNemar power is not determined by net lift alone.

     1	# Quantization-mismatch investigation — Stage 2 recommendation
     2	
     3	Date: 2026-07-06. Status: **recommendation = NARROW (proceed to a bounded Stage 2
     4	proof-of-concept; do not commit to a full fine-tuning pipeline).** Inputs:
     5	`summaries/quant_mismatch_diagnostic.md` (Stage 0) and `summaries/stage1_tap_precision.md`
     6	(Stage 1), both adversarial-codex-reviewed. This note is the deliverable for the
     7	issue468 quant-mismatch goal.
     8	
     9	## What was tested (Stage 0 + Stage 1, both codex-reviewed)
    10	
    11	- **Stage 0 (offline diagnostic, robust):** the DSpark drafter's p=1 misses vs the
    12	  IQ2XXS target are **shallow and in the right neighborhood** — median target-rank
    13	  on misses = 1.0; 100% within the drafter's top-10; top-2 coverage 0.8125→0.9125.
    14	  This is the regime where a fine-tune has maximum leverage. Causal link to *quant*
    15	  is NOT proven (only ~27% of misses are genuine Q2 near-ties; median Q2 gap 2.15 nat).
    16	- **Stage 1 (Q4-tap A/B, underpowered):** raising layers 37–42 routed experts to
    17	  Q4_K did **not materially improve p=1 acceptance** (0.8125→0.7875, McNemar p≈0.77;
    18	  E[a|5block] +0.10 with bootstrap 95% CI [−0.16, +0.41] — not proven noise, study
    19	  underpowered; one-sided deeper-position trend p3–p5, rollout-confounded). This
    20	  variant cannot isolate tap precision from lower-layer Q2, so it falsifies only
    21	  "this expert-only Q4-tap variant helps," not "quant mismatch" in general.
    22	
    23	## Recommendation: NARROW — a bounded Stage 2 proof-of-concept, not a full pipeline
    24	
    25	**Proceed to Stage 2 only as a small, bounded PoC**, gated on a measurable p=1 lift.
    26	Rationale:
    27	
    28	- **For:** Stage 0 robustly shows recoverable-shape (shallow) error with real
    29	  headroom (top-2 coverage 0.91 at p=1). Fine-tuning addresses the deficit
    30	  *regardless of root cause* (quant or calibration) by teaching the served target's
    31	  argmax ordering. And it is the **last unexplored lever with supporting evidence**:
    32	  drafter precision is exhausted (`dspark_quantization_ceiling.md`), the verifier is
    33	  bandwidth-bound (`mtp_verifier_bench_results.md`), trees don't help
    34	  (`spec_speedup_model.md` Q3), and DFlash is a worse drafter (`dflash_oracle_investigation.md`).
    35	- **Against / cautions:** the deficit's *cause* is unknown (lower-layer Q2,
    36	  calibration, or irreducible capacity). If it is capacity, fine-tuning has a low
    37	  ceiling. n=10 prompts / temp=0 only — the shallow-error finding needs broader
    38	  confirmation before a large investment. Fine-tuning is explicitly out of scope
    39	  for cycle 1 (GOAL.md), so this is a scope-extension decision the user should make
    40	  consciously.
    41	
    42	**Realistic ceiling — set expectations honestly (secondary gate, not primary):**
    43	Even a fine-tune that captured every current top-2 case (p=1 → ~0.91) reaches
    44	"beat baseline / match --mtp" at K=4 per the speedup model, but **not** the +20%
    45	primary gate (needs ~0.94 at K=4 / ~0.89 at K=5). The +20% gate is a **compound
    46	stretch**: it needs fine-tuning *and* the unbuilt anchor-reuse verifier
    47	(`spec_speedup_model.md` flags the shipped `--mtp` verifier pays a redundant anchor
    48	decode, ~−18 pp at K=4) *and* acceptance near the top-2 ceiling. So: fine-tuning
    49	most plausibly delivers the **secondary** gate; the primary gate is an outside shot
    50	requiring multiple independent things to land.
    51	
    52	## Recommended next experiments (ranked; cheap ones first)
    53	
    54	1. **Crossed hidden/label oracle (cheap, reuses existing artifacts).** Combine
    55	   Q4-tap hidden states with baseline target tokens, and baseline hidden states
    56	   with Q4-tap tokens, then re-measure. Separates **input-shift** (hidden-state
    57	   representation — fixable via the drafter's input projection) from **label-shift**
    58	   (argmax drift). Tells the fine-tune *where* to focus. No ds4 recapture.
    59	2. **Broader / temp-varied corpus for the Stage 0 diagnostic.** Re-run the rank
    60	   diagnostic on >100 prompts at temp 0/0.5/1.0 to confirm the shallow-error
    61	   finding and narrow the CIs before any ML spend.
    62	3. **Bounded Stage 2 PoC (the actual fine-tune test).** Small LoRA on a modest
    63	   Q2-distillation corpus, measured on the existing harness. Decision rule: a
    64	   **+3–5 pp p=1 lift** ⇒ the direction has legs (scale up); **flat** ⇒ the deficit
    65	   is closer to irreducible capacity than calibration ⇒ stop.
    66	4. **(Decisive but high-effort, needs a model not on disk)** Full Q8/BF16 target
    67	   top-k on the exact p=1 miss set — directly separates quant from calibration.
    68	   Codex's proposed decisive mechanism test.
    69	
    70	## Fine-tuning-setup insights (from this investigation)
    71	
    72	- **Corpus = (served-target tap hidden states → served-target greedy argmax) pairs.**
    73	  The existing capture tooling (`run_exactness_small_bundles.py`) already produces
    74	  exactly these (layer-40/41/42 hidden states + greedy tokens). Corpus gen reuses
    75	  it — just needs more / longer prompts and a train/eval split.
    76	- **The drafter's input is the concat of layers 40/41/42 (3·DIM=12288).** A minimal
    77	  viable fine-tune targets `main_proj` (input projection) + the 3 drafter dense
    78	  layers + the **markov head** (`markov_w1`/`markov_w2`). The markov head directly
    79	  controls the top-of-distribution ordering where Stage 0 showed the errors
    80	  concentrate (target usually rank 2); it must be in scope.
    81	- **Low LoRA rank may suffice.** The error is a consistent one-rank mis-ordering,
    82	  not a deep representation failure — suggesting a small parameter delta could move
    83	  the argmax. Start with a small rank and measure.
    84	- **Eval on the exactness corpus, exact-output preservation required.** Stage 2's
    85	  success bar is a p=1 lift that preserves greedy exactness on the retained
    86	  exactness bundles (the GOAL's exactness constraint). The harness for this exists.
    87	- **Risk to watch:** if the deficit originates in lower-layer Q2 (Stage 1 could not
    88	  rule this out), the fine-tune is learning to *compensate* for a representation
    89	  shift at its input — learnable, but the gain magnitude is unknown until measured.
    90	
    91	## What would change this recommendation
    92	
    93	- **Upgrade to "proceed (full)":** the crossed oracle (exp 1) shows the deficit is
    94	  predominantly input-side label-shift, AND a broader-corpus Stage 0 confirms
    95	  shallowness holds, AND the PoC (exp 3) clears +5 pp p=1.
    96	- **Downgrade to "stop":** the crossed oracle or a Q8 target test shows the deficit
    97	  is irreducible drafter capacity (target rarely in drafter top-k on a larger
    98	  corpus), OR the PoC is flat, OR temp>0 deployment collapses E[a] faster than
    99	  fine-tuning can recover.
   100	
   101	## One-line verdict
   102	
   103	The quant-mismatch hypothesis, as originally framed (FP-trained drafter vs Q2
   104	target, fixable by precision or fine-tuning), is **partially falsified** — tap
   105	precision doesn't help — but the **underlying shallow-error finding is robust and
   106	keeps a bounded drafter fine-tune in play as the last plausible lever**, most
   107	realistically targeting the secondary gate. NARROW.

   190	                id2logit, lp = q2_step_dist(topk, step + p)
   191	                q2_gap = float("nan")
   192	                if len(lp) >= 2:
   193	                    q2_gap = float(lp[0]["logit"] - lp[1]["logit"])
   194	                rdiq = rank_in_q2(drafter_argmax, id2logit, lp)
   195	                # audit capture: top-64 (token,score) + target score, so any rank<=64 is
   196	                # re-derivable from artifacts alone (count top64_scores > target_score).
   197	                order64 = np.argsort(-full_score, kind="stable")[:64]
   198	                audit_ids.append(order64.astype(np.int32))
   199	                audit_scores.append(full_score[order64].astype(np.float32))
   200	                audit_tgt_score.append(np.float32(full_score[target_tok]))
   201	                rows.append({
   202	                    "prompt": prompt, "step": step, "pos": pos, "p": p,
   203	                    "anchor": anchor, "prev_tok": prev_tok,
   204	                    "drafter_argmax": drafter_argmax, "target_tok": target_tok,
   205	                    "match": match, "rank_target_in_drafter": rank_target,
   206	                    "drafter_top1_top2_gap": round(drafter_gap, 4),
   207	                    "rank_drafter_in_q2": rdiq,
   208	                    "q2_top1_top2_gap": (round(q2_gap, 4) if q2_gap == q2_gap else None),
   209	                })
   210	
   211	        print(f"  {prompt}: {max_step} steps processed", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)
   212	
   213	    if crosscheck_failures:
   214	        print(f"\nABORT: {crosscheck_failures} reproduced-vs-retained draft mismatches; "
   215	              f"forward fidelity not established, ranks untrusted.", file=sys.stderr)
   216	        return 2
   217	
   218	    # ---- persist raw per-position rows ----
   219	    OUT_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
   220	    import csv
   221	    with (OUT_DIR / "per_position.csv").open("w", newline="") as f:
   222	        w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(rows[0].keys()))
   223	        w.writeheader()
   224	        w.writerows(rows)
   225	    (OUT_DIR / "per_position.json").write_text(json.dumps(rows, indent=2) + "\n")

    33	def detect_positions(captures_dir: Path) -> list[int]:
    34	    npz = capture_npz_path(captures_dir)
    35	    if npz.exists():
    36	        data = np.load(npz)
    37	        return [int(v) for v in data["positions"].tolist()]
    38	    positions = set()
    39	    for path in captures_dir.rglob("dump_hc_ffn_post-*_pos*.bin"):
    40	        tail = path.stem.split("_pos")[-1]
    41	        if tail.isdigit():
    42	            positions.add(int(tail))
    43	    return sorted(positions)

    46	def load_or_build_capture_arrays(captures_dir: Path) -> tuple[list[int], dict[int, np.ndarray]]:
    47	    npz = capture_npz_path(captures_dir)
    48	    if npz.exists():
    49	        data = np.load(npz)
    50	        positions = [int(v) for v in data["positions"].tolist()]
    51	        layer_arrays = {
    52	            40: data["layer40"],
    53	            41: data["layer41"],
    54	            42: data["layer42"],
    55	        }
    56	        return positions, layer_arrays
    57	
    58	    positions = [p for p in detect_positions(captures_dir) if p != 0]
    59	    layer_lists: dict[int, list[np.ndarray]] = {layer: [] for layer in LAYERS}
    60	    for pos in positions:
    61	        for layer in LAYERS:
    62	            matches = sorted(captures_dir.rglob(f"dump_hc_ffn_post-{layer}_pos{pos}.bin"))
    63	            if len(matches) != 1:
    64	                raise FileNotFoundError(f"expected exactly one capture for layer={layer} pos={pos}, found {len(matches)}")
    65	            path = matches[0]
    66	            arr = np.fromfile(path, dtype=np.float32)
    67	            if arr.size != HC * DIM:
    68	                raise ValueError(f"unexpected capture size for {path}: {arr.size} (wanted {HC * DIM})")
    69	            layer_lists[layer].append(arr.reshape(HC, DIM))
    70	    layer_arrays = {layer: np.stack(layer_lists[layer], axis=0) for layer in LAYERS}
    71	    np.savez(

issue468/ref/DSpark_paper.md:406:Speculative decoding places a further demand that the drafter must provide exact per-token probabilities for the rejection sampling rule. Most techniques above cannot readily provide such probabilities due to iterative refinement, latent marginalization, or global normalization. For instance, in a design closely related to ours, CRF-NAT (Sun et al., 2019) also places a sequential module over parallel hidden states, but its globally normalized partition function prevents exact per-token probability computation. Similarly, when adapting the CTC output layer to parallel speculative decoding, CTC-drafter (Wen et al., 2024) is restricted to greedy verification due to the latent marginalization of alignment paths. DSpark circumvents these limitations by keeping the sequential correction local, so per-token probabilities remain exact softmax evaluations.

   157	Prior methods (Huang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b) typically apply a static threshold to confidence scores to determine verification length. While effective under isolated, single-request assumptions, static thresholds can be suboptimal in high-concurrency production systems, where the utility of verifying a draft token depends heavily on the current system load. 
   158	
   159	To address this, we formulate verification length selection as a global throughput maximization problem (Algorithm 1). Consider a batch of _𝑅_ active requests. For request _𝑟_ , let _𝑐𝑟_ ,1, _. . ._ , _𝑐𝑟_ , _𝛾_ be the per-position confidence estimates, and let _ℓ𝑟_ ∈{0, _. . ._ , _𝛾_ } denote the scheduled verification length. Because speculative decoding dynamically accepts draft tokens only as a continuous prefix, the survival probability of a token at position _𝑗_ is the cumulative product _𝑎𝑟_ , _𝑗_ =[�] _𝑖_ ⩽ _𝑗[𝑐][𝑟]_ , _[𝑖]_[.] 
   160	
   161	In a single verification step, the total batch size (measured in tokens) sent to the target model is _𝐵_ =[�] _𝑟[𝑅]_ =1[(][1][ +] _[ ℓ][𝑟]_[)][,][and][the][expected][number][of][successfully][accepted][tokens][is] _[𝜏]_[=] � _𝑟𝑅_ =1 �1 + � _ℓ𝑗_ = _𝑟_ 1 _[𝑎][𝑟]_[,] _[𝑗]_ �. Let SPS( _𝐵_ ) denote the engine throughput, measured in steps per second, for _𝐵_ . a given forward-pass batch size Crucially, this capacity curve is profiled once during engine initialization and stored as a lightweight cost table. Our scheduler then aims to maximize the expected system-wide token throughput Θ = _𝜏_ · SPS( _𝐵_ ) by dynamically selecting verification lengths _ℓ_ 1, _. . ._ , _ℓ𝑅_ . 
   162	
   163	Although finding the global maximum of Θ appears to be a combinatorial search, the objective structure allows for an efficient greedy solution. Because _𝑎𝑟_ , _𝑗_ is monotonically nonincreasing with respect to _𝑗_ (i.e., _𝑎𝑟_ , _𝑗_ ≤ _𝑎𝑟_ , _𝑗_ −1), the marginal gain in expected accepted tokens for extending request _𝑟_ ’s verification length from _𝑗_ − 1 to _𝑗_ is exactly _𝑎𝑟_ , _𝑗_ . This monotonicity ensures that sorting candidate tokens globally by _𝑎𝑟_ , _𝑗_ naturally respects intra-block prefix dependencies. Consequently, if the total verification batch size _𝐵_ were fixed, the optimal allocation { _ℓ𝑟_ } would be determined by greedily selecting the draft tokens with the highest survival probabilities from the global pool of all { _𝑎𝑟_ , _𝑗_ }. 
   164	
   165	Building on this insight, the optimization can be evaluated along this greedy admission path. 
   166	
   167	8 
   168	
   169	We first globally sort all valid prefix extensions in descending order of survival probability. To dynamically determine the optimal target batch size _𝐵_ , we incrementally admit tokens from this sorted pool, updating the expected throughput Θ via an _𝑂_ (1) lookup from the pre-profiled cost table. 
   170	
   171	Lossless speculative decoding strictly requires the _non-anticipating property_ : admission decisions must not depend on future candidate tokens (Chen et al., 2023; Leviathan et al., 2023). Because our confidence head relies on the Markov feature of the previously sampled token, computing the next survival probability _𝑎𝑟_ , _𝑘_ +1 explicitly requires the instantiated candidate _𝑥𝑟_ , _𝑘_ . A retrospective global search would thus inadvertently leak _𝑥𝑟_ , _𝑘_ into the admission decision for step _𝑘_ , introducing selection bias (we provide a concrete counterexample demonstrating this theoretical violation in Appendix A). 
   172	
   173	To enforce strict causality, the scheduler (Algorithm 1) employs an early-stopping mechanism. By breaking the greedy search immediately when the throughput drops (Θ ≤ Θbest), the truncation decision relies solely on the prefix processed up to that exact step. This isolates the admission event from future tokens, ensuring exact target-distribution recovery. Note that this stepwise early-stopping yields the global maximum throughput if and only if the objective Θ is unimodal, which implicitly assumes a smoothly decaying hardware capacity curve. We address the engineering adaptations required for real-world, non-smooth SPS characteristics and asynchronous system pipelines in Section 5.2. 
   174	
   175	## **3.3. Training** 
   176	
   177	During training, we randomly sample multiple anchor positions from each target sequence to form _𝛾_ -token blocks as training data. The target model is frozen throughout training; the draft model shares its embedding layer and language modeling head and keeps them frozen, updating only the backbone drafter, sequential block, and confidence head. 
   178	
   179	The training objective consists of three terms: a cross-entropy loss Lce, a distributionmatching loss Ltv, and a confidence loss Lconf. All three are position-weighted by _𝑤𝑘_ = exp(−( _𝑘_ −1)/ _𝛾_ ) (Chen et al., 2026), which emphasizes earlier block positions that contribute more to the expected acceptance length under prefix-based verification.    197	In this section, we validate the draft quality of DSpark using offline benchmarks and report the effectiveness of confidence scheduler under online production traffic in Section 5. The experimental setup is described in Section 4.1, main results in Section 4.2, and additional analyses are included in Section 4.3. 
   198	
   199	## **4.1. Experimental Setup** 
   200	
   201	**Target and draft models.** We evaluate DSpark on four target models spanning different scales and model families: Qwen3-{4B, 8B, 14B} (Yang et al., 2025), and Gemma4-12B (Google DeepMind, 2026). For draft models, we compare DSpark with two representative drafters: DFlash (Chen et al., 2026), a state-of-the-art parallel drafter, and Eagle3 (Li et al., 2026b), an autoregressive drafter based on Training-Time Test (TTT). For fair comparison, we retrain all drafters in the same training framework and on the same data. We align Eagle3’s TTT horizon (7) with the block size (7) used by DFlash and DSpark, and we use the same target-model feature layers for all drafters. For the number of draft model layers, we set 1 for Eagle3 and 5 for DSpark and DFlash (Chen et al., 2026). Unless otherwise stated, DSpark denotes the Markov-head variant; we study the RNN-head variant in Section 4.3.2. 
   202	
   203	**Training data.** We use Open-PerfectBlend[2] , an open-sourced version of PerfectBlend (Xu et al., 2024) consisting of 1.3 million samples. It is a general-purpose instruction dataset containing chat (17.6%), math (39.4%), code (38.9%), and instruction-following data (4.1%). We only use the prompts from Open-PerfectBlend; responses are regenerated by each target model with recommended sampling parameters. Each drafter is trained for 10 epochs to ensure full convergence. For data generation and evaluation, we adopt the non-thinking mode. 
   204	
   205	**Evaluation protocol.** We evaluate the performance of different algorithms on three domains: 
   206	
   207	1. **Mathematical Reasoning** , including GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2024) and AIME25 (Zhang and Math-AI, 2025). 
   208	
   209	2. **Code Generation** , including MBPP (Austin et al., 2021b), HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) and Live-CodeBench (Jain et al., 2025). 
   210	
   211	3. **Daily Chat** , including MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2023), Alpaca (Taori et al., 2023) and Arena-Hard (Li et al., 2024a, 2025b). 
   212	
   213	For all benchmarks, we use standard speculative decoding (Chen et al., 2023; Leviathan et al., 2023) with the sampling temperature set to 1.0. We report the accepted length ( _𝜏_ ) per decoding round[3] . For all drafters, we use chain-based drafting.

   393	
   394	## **6. Related Work** 
   395	
   396	**Speculative Decoding Algorithms.** Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by decoupling token proposal from verification. Building on early blockwise methods (Ge et al., 2022; Stern et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2021; Xia et al., 2023), modern approaches employ rejection sampling to exactly preserve the target model’s distribution (Chen et al., 2023; Leviathan et al., 2023). Because inference speedup directly depends on the drafter’s efficiency and accuracy, extensive research has focused on optimizing its architecture. Beyond using standalone small language models (Chen et al., 2023; Leviathan et al., 2023), subsequent work integrates multi-token heads or feature extrapolators directly into the target model (Ankner et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2024, 2025; DeepSeek-AI, 2024; Gloeckle et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b,c, 2026b; Zhang et al., 2025). Other strategies include self-speculation via early exits (Elhoushi et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024a; Xia et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024), dynamic vocabulary compression (Williams et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2025b), prompt lookup (Saxena, 2023; Somasundaram et al., 2025), suffix automata (Hu et al., 2025), and retrieval (He et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2026). To remove the sequential bottleneck of drafting itself, recent methods propose parallel or blockwise generation. P-EAGLE parallelizes EAGLE-style drafting (Hui et al., 2026), while PARD, DART, and DFlash use diffusion-inspired prediction to generate entire blocks in a single forward pass (An et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a), which DDTree then extends into verifiable draft trees (Ringel and Romano, 2026). Concurrent efforts also improve DFlash: Domino (Huang et al., 2026a) introduces a CausalEncoder conceptually similar to our RNN Head, while DFlare (Zhang et al., 2026a) addresses conditioning bottlenecks via layer-wise fusion. 
   397	
   398	**System-Aware Scheduling for Speculative Decoding.** Beyond drafter architecture, another line of work focuses on determining the optimal number of speculative tokens to generate or verify in each round. To this end, various approaches adapt draft lengths on the fly using confidence heuristics (Du et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2026c; Mamou et al., 2024; Wen and Feng, 2026), learned acceptance predictors (Huang et al., 2024; Zacks917, 2026), or bandit-style policies (Liu et al., 2026b). Furthermore, recognizing speculative decoding as inherently a systemlevel scheduling problem, recent works optimize overall goodput and latency by adjusting speculation budgets according to real-time system load and request priority (AngelSlim Team, 2026; Hu et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2024c; Miao et al., 2024; Sadhukhan et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025). 
   399	
   400	**Parallel Generation.** Models that generate tokens in parallel offer a decoding latency nearly independent of output length, making them an attractive alternative to autoregressive decoding. Non-Autoregressive Transformers (NATs, Gu et al., 2018) pioneered this direction by predicting all positions independently in a single pass. However, this forces the model to average over all 
   401	
   402	20 
   403	
   404	plausible modes, often producing outputs that mix fragments from different valid sequences. Two broad lines of work have emerged to address this limitation. One direction retains the single-pass architecture but changes what the model sees or how it is trained: introducing latent variables as conditioning input to steer all positions toward a consistent output (Gu et al., 2018; Kaiser et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2019), or relaxing the training objective so that the model focuses on producing a single coherent output rather than modeling the full distribution over all valid alternatives (Du et al., 2021; Qian et al., 2021; Shao et al., 2021, 2023). The other direction reintroduces limited sequential dependency through iterative re-prediction (Austin et al., 2021a; Ghazvininejad et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022), block-level autoregression (Arriola et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2018), or structured output layers such as CRF (Sun et al., 2019), CTC (Libovický and Helcl, 2018; Saharia et al., 2020), HMM (Huang et al., 2022b), and PCFG (Gui et al., 2023). 
   405	
   406	Speculative decoding places a further demand that the drafter must provide exact per-token probabilities for the rejection sampling rule. Most techniques above cannot readily provide such probabilities due to iterative refinement, latent marginalization, or global normalization. For instance, in a design closely related to ours, CRF-NAT (Sun et al., 2019) also places a sequential module over parallel hidden states, but its globally normalized partition function prevents exact per-token probability computation. Similarly, when adapting the CTC output layer to parallel speculative decoding, CTC-drafter (Wen et al., 2024) is restricted to greedy verification due to the latent marginalization of alignment paths. DSpark circumvents these limitations by keeping the sequential correction local, so per-token probabilities remain exact softmax evaluations. 
   407	
   408	## **7. Conclusion** 
   409	
   410	In this paper, we present DSpark, a speculative decoding framework designed to overcome the structural and system-level bottlenecks of large language model inference in high-concurrency production environments. Algorithmically, DSpark introduces a semi-autoregressive generation paradigm—coupling a computationally heavy parallel backbone with a lightweight sequential head—to mitigate the rapid suffix decay of independent parallel drafters. At the system level, we formulate verification length selection as a global throughput maximization problem, employing a hardware-aware prefix scheduler that dynamically tailors the target model’s verification budget based on calibrated survival probabilities and real-time engine load. Extensive offline evaluations demonstrate that DSpark substantially outperforms state-of-the-art autoregressive and parallel baselines across diverse domains. Furthermore, its real-world deployment within the DeepSeek-V4 validates its practical value in production serving: by intelligently managing verification overhead, DSpark sustains robust concurrency under heavy load, consistently accelerates per-user generation speeds, and effectively shifts the Pareto frontier of LLM serving outward.

9:Speculative decoding accelerates Large Language Model (LLM) inference by decoupling draft generation from target verification. While recent parallel drafters efficiently propose long token sequences in a single forward pass, they suffer from rapid acceptance decay due to a lack of inter-token dependencies. Furthermore, indiscriminately verifying these extended blocks wastes critical batch capacity on tokens with high rejection risks, severely degrading throughput in high-concurrency serving systems. We introduce DSpark, a speculative decoding framework that unifies high-throughput parallel generation with adaptive, load-aware verification. To maintain draft quality, DSpark utilizes a semi-autoregressive architecture—coupling a parallel backbone with a lightweight sequential module—to introduce intra-block dependency modeling and mitigate suffix decay. To optimize system efficiency, DSpark employs confidence-scheduled verification, dynamically tailoring the verification length for each request based on estimated prefix survival probabilities and engine-specific throughput profiles. On offline benchmarks across diverse domains, DSpark substantially improves the accepted length over state-of-the-art autoregressive and parallel drafters. When deployed within the DeepSeek-V4 serving system under live user traffic, DSpark successfully mitigates verification waste. Compared to the established production baseline (MTP-1), DSpark accelerates per-user generation speeds by 60%–85% at matched throughput levels. More importantly, by preventing severe throughput degradation under strict interactivity constraints, it enables performance tiers that were previously unattainable, shifting the Pareto frontier of our serving system. To facilitate community progress, we open-source the DSpark checkpoints alongside DeepSpec, an algorithm-driven training repository for speculative decoding. 
17:a primary bottleneck in production LLM serving, particularly for latency-sensitive scenarios such as real-time conversational assistants and multi-turn agentic workflows. Speculative decoding (Chen et al., 2023; Leviathan et al., 2023) offers a principled solution: a lightweight _draft model_ proposes a block of candidate tokens, and the full-size _target model_ verifies the entire block in a single forward pass via rejection sampling, accepting the longest prefix consistent with the target distribution and appending one bonus token. Because verification is parallel and the acceptance rule preserves the target distribution exactly, speculative decoding accelerates generation without any quality loss. 
19:The design of the draft model governs the trade-off between drafting latency and acceptance rate. Early drafters are autoregressive (Cheng et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b), conditioning each position on previously sampled tokens. However, their drafting latency grows linearly with the block size, forcing these methods to use short blocks and shallow architectures. To break this sequential bottleneck, parallel drafters (Cai et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a) have emerged as a compelling alternative: all draft positions are produced in a single forward pass, making drafting latency nearly independent of block size. This structural advantage theoretically allows parallel drafters to efficiently generate substantially longer draft blocks. 
21:However, fully unlocking the potential of large parallel draft blocks introduces two critical bottlenecks—one in generation quality, and the other in system efficiency. First, because parallel drafters predict each position independently, they cannot model inter-token dependencies within a block. This independence leads to multi-modal collisions and rapid acceptance decay at later positions (Gu et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2022b). Second, determining the optimal verification length remains a challenge. While parallel generation easily produces long draft blocks, indiscriminately verifying all proposed tokens degrades system throughput, particularly under high-concurrency workloads (Hu et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2024c). The ideal verification length varies along two axes. On the data side, structured requests like code naturally sustain higher acceptance rates than open-ended chat (Abramovich et al., 2026; Xia et al., 2024). On the system side, verifying extra tokens is nearly free under light loads. Under heavy loads, however, verifying tokens with a high rejection risk occupies critical batch capacity that could otherwise serve other active requests (Liu et al., 2024b; Wu et al., 2025).

131:This performance bottleneck stems from two interacting factors. First, on the data side, draft acceptance rates inherently vary across domains: structured text like code naturally yields high acceptance, whereas open-ended chat has significantly lower acceptance (Abramovich et al., 2026; Xia et al., 2024). Second, on the system side, the actual cost of verifying an extra token depends strictly on the engine load. Under light system load, an extra verification incurs minimal penalty even if rejected. However, under high-concurrency deployments, every unnecessary verification occupies target model batch capacity that could otherwise serve other active requests (Liu et al., 2024b; Wu et al., 2025).

145:**Post-hoc Calibration.** Unlike threshold-based verification heuristics (Huang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b; Zhang et al., 2026b), which only require confidence scores to correctly rank draft token qualities, our hardware-aware scheduling approach (detailed in Section 3.2.2) precisely requires the absolute magnitudes of the cumulative acceptance probabilities to compute the expected acceptance length _𝜏_ . Because neural confidence estimates are often overconfident (Guo et al., 2017; Ovadia et al., 2019), using the raw confidence scores directly would distort the throughput estimation, leading to suboptimal scheduling. 
147:To address this, we introduce **Sequential Temperature Scaling (STS)** . Because each _𝑐𝑖_ models a conditional probability, the chain rule dictates that the joint probability of a draft prefix being accepted factorizes into the cumulative product[�] _𝑖_ ⩽ _𝑘[𝑐][𝑖]_[.][Using a held-out validation set, STS] calibrates this joint probability consecutively from left to right. Specifically, at each position _𝑘_ ∈{1, _. . ._ , _𝛾_ }, we perform a simple 1D grid search to find the optimal temperature scalar that minimizes the Expected Calibration Error (ECE) (Naeini et al., 2015) of the cumulative product, keeping the already-calibrated scores of all preceding positions fixed. Crucially, temperature scaling is an order-preserving transformation: it rectifies the predicted probabilities to match empirical acceptance rates without disrupting the relative draft token rankings learned by the confidence head. 
163:Although finding the global maximum of Θ appears to be a combinatorial search, the objective structure allows for an efficient greedy solution. This monotonicity ensures that sorting candidate tokens globally by _𝑎𝑟_ , _𝑗_ naturally respects intra-block prefix dependencies. Consequently, if the total verification batch size _𝐵_ were fixed, the optimal allocation { _ℓ𝑟_ } would be determined by greedily selecting the draft tokens with the highest survival probabilities from the global pool of all { _𝑎𝑟_ , _𝑗_ }.

173:To enforce strict causality, the scheduler (Algorithm 1) employs an early-stopping mechanism. By breaking the greedy search immediately when the throughput drops (Θ ≤ Θbest), the truncation decision relies solely on the prefix processed up to that exact step. This isolates the admission event from future tokens, ensuring exact target-distribution recovery. Note that this stepwise early-stopping yields the global maximum throughput if and only if the objective Θ is unimodal, which implicitly assumes a smoothly decaying hardware capacity curve. 258:**The Capacity Advantage at Position 1.** At the first draft position, both architectures predict the next token based solely on the target context. The performance divergence here stems strictly from architectural capacity: autoregressive models like Eagle3 are constrained to shallow networks due to their _𝑂_ ( _𝛾_ ) latency, whereas _𝑂_ (1) parallel drafters can afford much deeper networks. This structural gap yields a substantial accuracy margin at position 1, with DFlash starting noticeably higher than Eagle3 (e.g., 0.88 vs. 0.81 on Math, and 0.72 vs. 0.53 on Chat). Because speculative decoding operates as a strict prefix-matching survival process, the first token carries the highest leverage—a rejection here immediately invalidates the entire block. Consequently, this initial capacity advantage disproportionately boosts the final accepted length, explaining why parallel drafters ultimately outperform autoregressive ones globally despite rapid acceptance decay at later positions. 
260:**The Limitation of Independence at Later Positions.** Examining the tail of the curves (positions 2 through 7) exposes the inherent limitation of independent parallel generation. As earlier tokens lock in a specific semantic path, subsequent tokens naturally become more predictable. Autoregressive models like Eagle3 effectively leverage this conditional certainty, maintaining or even increasing conditional acceptance deeper into the block (e.g., from 0.53 to 0.74 on Chat). In contrast, DFlash suffers from rapid acceptance decay, dropping from 0.87 to 0.78 on Code and 0.72 to 0.63 on Chat. Because each parallel position marginalizes over all possible prior tokens rather than conditioning on an exact sampled prefix, the model frequently proposes inconsistent suffix combinations—a mode known as multi-modal collision (Gu et al., 2018; Stern et al., 2018). 
276:motivates DSpark’s semi-autoregressive design. As shown in Figure 2, DSpark inherits the high initial acceptance of the deep parallel drafter (e.g., starting at 0.93 on Math). Simultaneously, its lightweight sequential head mitigates the rapid acceptance decay typical of parallel generation. By resolving this trade-off, DSpark maintains a high and stable conditional acceptance rate throughout the entire draft block.
